newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. rebuffs EU bid for WTO panel on Cuba trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rebuffs EU bid for WTO panel on Cuba trade.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday blocked a European Union request for a World Trade Organisation (WTO) panel to rule on Washington's controversial Helms-Burton investment law which penalises firms doing business with Cuba.

But, under the rules of the Geneva-based WTO, a neutral panel on the dispute will be created automatically at the next regular meeting of the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body on November 20 -- just over two weeks after the U.S. presidential and congressional elections on November 5.

A WTO member state can only refuse once to the setting up of a panel and must agree the second time. This was the EU's first request and it followed three rounds of bilateral consultations since June.

The European Commission, the EU's Brussels-based executive, said in a statement the bloc objected to the United States "trying to force other countries to follow their own foreign policy objectives through the threat and actual imposition of trade sanctions".

The Helms-Burton law, which has been condemned by all major U.S. trading partners, including Canada and Mexico, allows U.S. citizens to sue foreign firms which invest in property confiscated after Cuba's revolution in 1959.
In the transatlantic row, the EU argues that the legislation violates trade rules while Washington supports it, saying it is a matter of national security.
The Commission's statement, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, was read by Ian Wilkinson, acting head of the EU trade delegation in Geneva, to a closed-door session of the WTO.
The EU said it opposed U.S. "exerting jurisdiction" over European-registered but U.S.-controlled companies.
Washington, which has tried to dissuade the EU from going ahead with a WTO panel, has indicated it may invoke the never-tested national security exemption in its defence.

If the neutral panel rules that Washington may invoke its exemption on grounds of national security interests, it could set a damaging precedent that could jeopardise WTO non-discrimination rules, trade sources say.
